chapters.title: Motion in 2D
chapters.description: How objects move in two dimensions, including projectiles, circular motion, rotation, and gravity.

lessons.title: Motion in Two Dimensions
lessons.summary: Learn how projectiles move through the air by treating horizontal and vertical motion separately. Also explore circular motion and gravity.

sections.title: Why study motion in 2D?
sections.body:
In Grade 9 you studied motion in a straight line (one dimension). But most real motion happens in **two dimensions (2D)**. When you kick a football, throw a stone, or watch water arc out of a hose, the object moves both **forward (horizontal)** and **up or down (vertical)** at the same time.

A **projectile** is any object thrown or launched through the air that moves only under the pull of gravity (no engine pushing it). The clever trick that physicists use is this: we split the motion into a **horizontal part** and a **vertical part**, then solve each part on its own. This works because the two directions do not affect each other.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define a **projectile** and give examples.
- Explain the difference between **1D** and **2D** motion.
- Use the terms **angle of elevation** and **angle of depression** correctly.
- Describe how gravity changes the **vertical velocity** but not the **horizontal velocity**.
- Use the equations of uniform acceleration to find **flight time**, **range**, and **maximum height**.
- Define **centre of mass** and **centripetal force**, and calculate centripetal force.

sections.title: Horizontal and vertical motion
sections.body:
The key idea is **independence of motion**: horizontal and vertical motion happen at the same time but do not influence each other.

**Horizontal motion:** If we ignore air resistance, there is no horizontal force on a projectile once it is launched. With no force there is no acceleration, so the **horizontal velocity stays constant** for the whole flight. We use:

`horizontal displacement = horizontal velocity × flight time`

**Vertical motion:** Gravity pulls everything downward, giving an acceleration of **g = 9.81 m/s²** (Standard Gravity). So the **vertical velocity keeps changing**. On the way up the object slows down, reaches zero vertical velocity at the top, then speeds up on the way down. This is *uniformly accelerated motion*, so we can use the five equations of motion:

1. `v = u + at`
2. `s = ½(u + v)t`
3. `s = ut + ½at²`
4. `v² = u² + 2as`
5. `s = vt − ½at²`

Here **s** = displacement, **u** = initial velocity, **v** = final velocity, **a** = acceleration, **t** = time.

**Why does the path curve?** Because the horizontal velocity is steady while the vertical velocity speeds up, the combined path bends into a special curve called a **parabola**.

**Resolving velocity:** When a projectile is launched at an angle θ, we split its launch velocity *u* into parts using trigonometry:
- Horizontal component: `uₓ = u cos θ`
- Vertical component: `u_y = u sin θ`

**Angles:** An angle measured *above* the horizontal is the **angle of elevation**; an angle measured *below* the horizontal is the **angle of depression**.

**Useful results** (launch from ground level, ignoring air resistance):
- Time to maximum height: `t = (u sin θ) / g`
- Total flight time: `T = (2u sin θ) / g`
- Range: `R = (u² sin 2θ) / g`
- Maximum range happens at **θ = 45°**, where `R = u² / g`.

**Centre of mass:** The **centre of mass** is the single point where all the mass of an object can be thought of as concentrated. For a uniform shape it is at the centre. A force acting through this point causes no turning.

**Uniform circular motion:** This is movement along a circle of constant radius at constant speed. Even though the speed is constant, the **velocity changes** because the direction keeps changing. A changing velocity means there is an acceleration, which needs a force. This inward force is the **centripetal force**, always pointing toward the centre:

`F = mv² / r`

where **m** = mass, **v** = speed, **r** = radius.

sections.title: Worked example: ball kicked at an angle
sections.body:
**Problem:** A football is kicked from the ground at **20 m/s** at an angle of **30°** above the horizontal. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find (a) the maximum height, and (b) the horizontal range.

**Step 1 — Resolve the launch velocity into components.**
Vertical: `u_y = u sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s`
Horizontal: `uₓ = u cos θ = 20 × cos 30° = 20 × 0.866 = 17.3 m/s`

**Step 2 — Find the maximum height.** At the top, the vertical velocity is 0. Use `v² = u² − 2gs` (taking up as positive):
`0 = (10)² − 2 × 9.81 × s`
`0 = 100 − 19.62 s`
`s = 100 / 19.62 = 5.1 m`
So the **maximum height ≈ 5.1 m**.

**Step 3 — Find the total flight time.** Use `T = (2u sin θ) / g`:
`T = (2 × 10) / 9.81 = 20 / 9.81 = 2.04 s`

**Step 4 — Find the range.** Horizontal velocity stays constant:
`R = uₓ × T = 17.3 × 2.04 = 35.3 m`
So the **range ≈ 35 m**.

**Check:** Using the range equation `R = u² sin 2θ / g = 400 × sin 60° / 9.81 = 400 × 0.866 / 9.81 = 35.3 m`. The two methods agree.

sections.title: Vertical velocity of a falling ball
sections.body: This graph shows how the **downward velocity** of a dropped ball grows steadily over time. The straight line means the acceleration is constant at g = 9.81 m/s². Notice that after about 1 second the speed is roughly 9.8 m/s, and after 2 seconds it is about 19.6 m/s.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Mixing up directions.** You must pick one direction (up or down) as positive and stay with it for the whole problem. If down is positive, an upward launch velocity must be written as a **negative** number.
- **Thinking horizontal velocity slows down.** Ignoring air resistance, the **horizontal velocity never changes** during flight. Only the vertical velocity changes.
- **Believing heavier objects fall faster.** Without air resistance, all objects accelerate at the same rate (9.81 m/s²). A heavy stone and a light stone dropped together land together.
- **Forgetting to resolve the velocity.** For a launch at an angle, you cannot use the full speed for vertical calculations — you must first find `u sin θ`.
- **Using the wrong equation.** Pick the equation that does not contain the unknown you are *not* asked for. For example, if you do not know time, use `v² = u² + 2as`.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"SOH-CAH-TOA"** reminds you that the **S**in part is **vertical** (sin → up) and the **cos** part is **horizontal**: *vertical = u sin θ, horizontal = u cos θ*.
- Remember **"45 is the king of range"** — the longest range on flat ground is always at 45°.
- **"Time up = time down"**: for a projectile launched and landing at the same height, the rising time equals the falling time, so total time is double the time to the top.
- For circular motion, **"mv-squared-over-r"** is the chant for centripetal force: F = mv²/r.
- Picture a **monkey dropping a coconut while a hunter fires horizontally** — both hit the ground at the same instant, because vertical fall time depends only on height.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A ball is dropped from a height of 5.0 m. How long does it take to hit the ground? (Use g = 9.81 m/s².)

**Q2.** A stone is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s from a cliff. After 2.0 s, how far has it travelled horizontally?

**Q3.** A car of mass 1000 kg goes around a bend of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. What centripetal force is needed?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** Use `s = ½gt²` → `5.0 = ½ × 9.81 × t²` → `t² = 1.02` → **t ≈ 1.0 s**.
- **A2.** `horizontal distance = velocity × time = 8.0 × 2.0 =` **16 m**.
- **A3.** `F = mv²/r = 1000 × (20)² / 50 = 1000 × 400 / 50 =` **8000 N**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- A **projectile** moves under gravity alone; treat its **horizontal** and **vertical** motion separately.
- **Horizontal velocity is constant**; **vertical velocity changes** at g = 9.81 m/s².
- The path of a projectile is a **parabola**.
- Resolve a launch velocity: `uₓ = u cos θ`, `u_y = u sin θ`.
- Flight time `T = 2u sin θ / g`; range `R = u² sin 2θ / g`; **maximum range at 45°**.
- The **centre of mass** is where all mass can be treated as concentrated.
- **Uniform circular motion** needs a **centripetal force** `F = mv²/r` pointing to the centre.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: Any object moving through the air under the influence of gravity only, with no engine or driving force.
The curved (arch-shaped) path that a projectile follows through the air.
Splitting one vector into a horizontal and a vertical component that together have the same effect.
The angle of a launch measured above the horizontal.
The angle of a path measured below the horizontal.
The single point at which all the mass of an object can be considered to be concentrated.
The inward net force that keeps an object moving along a circular path, given by F = mv²/r.

flashcards.front: What is a projectile?
flashcards.back: Any object moving through the air under gravity alone, with no engine or driving force (e.g. a thrown stone or kicked ball).

flashcards.front: What happens to the horizontal velocity of a projectile (ignoring air resistance)?
flashcards.back: It stays constant for the whole flight, because there is no horizontal force.

flashcards.front: How do you resolve a launch velocity u at angle θ?
flashcards.back: Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ. Vertical: u_y = u sin θ.

flashcards.front: At what launch angle is the range greatest on flat ground?
flashcards.back: 45°, where range R = u² / g.

flashcards.front: What is the formula for centripetal force?
flashcards.back: F = mv² / r, directed toward the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: Ignoring air resistance, what happens to the horizontal velocity of a projectile during its flight?
options: It becomes zero at the top
questions.explanation: With no horizontal force there is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate acceleration due to gravity (Standard Gravity) used in these calculations?
questions.explanation: Standard Gravity is about 9.81 m/s², the rate at which objects accelerate downward near Earth's surface when air resistance is ignored.

questions.prompt: A ball is launched at 10 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. What is its initial vertical velocity component?
questions.explanation: Vertical component = u sin θ = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5.0 m/s.

questions.prompt: On flat ground and ignoring air resistance, which launch angle gives the greatest horizontal range?
questions.explanation: The range R = u² sin 2θ / g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, which happens at 2θ = 90°, so θ = 45°.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at a speed of 3.0 m/s. What is the centripetal force?
A stone is thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s. Using g = 9.8 m/s², how long does it take to reach its highest point?
questions.explanation: At the top, final vertical velocity is 0. Using v = u − gt: 0 = 19.6 − 9.8t, so t = 19.6 / 9.8 = 2.0 s.

chapters.title: Electrostatics
chapters.description: The study of electric charges at rest, the forces between them, electric fields, potential, and capacitors.

lessons.title: Electric Charge, Fields and Capacitors
lessons.summary: Discover how electric charges attract and repel, how to calculate the force and field around a charge, and how capacitors store charge.

sections.title: Electricity at rest
sections.body:
Have you ever rubbed a plastic pen on your hair and used it to pick up tiny pieces of paper? Or felt a small shock after walking across a dry floor? These are examples of **static electricity** — electric charge that stays in one place.

**Electrostatics** is the study of electric charges that are *not moving*. Everything around us is made of atoms, and atoms contain charged particles: **protons** (positive) and **electrons** (negative). When we rub two materials together, electrons can move from one to the other, leaving one object positively charged and the other negatively charged.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- State that there are two types of charge and describe how they interact.
- State and use **Coulomb's law** to find the force between two charges.
- Define and describe an **electric field** and calculate its strength.
- Explain **electric potential** and **potential difference (voltage)**.
- Define **capacitance** and use the formula `C = Q / V`.

sections.title: Charge, force, field, and capacitance
sections.body:
**Electric charge** is a basic property of matter. Its SI unit is the **coulomb (C)**. There are two kinds:
- **Positive charge** (carried by protons)
- **Negative charge** (carried by electrons)

The golden rule is: **like charges repel, unlike charges attract.** Two positive charges push apart; a positive and a negative charge pull together.

**Coulomb's law** tells us how strong the force is between two point charges:

`F = k × (q₁ × q₂) / r²`

where **F** = force (N), **q₁** and **q₂** = the two charges (C), **r** = distance between them (m), and **k** ≈ **9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²** (Coulomb's constant). Notice the force gets weaker very fast as the distance grows — doubling the distance makes the force **four times** smaller (an inverse-square law).

**Electric field:** A charge creates an invisible region of influence called an **electric field** around it. The field strength **E** is the force felt per unit positive charge:

`E = F / q`  (unit: newton per coulomb, N/C)

The field around a single point charge is `E = kQ / r²`. Field lines point **away from** positive charges and **toward** negative charges.

**Electric potential and voltage:** **Electric potential** is the electrical potential energy per unit charge at a point. The **potential difference (V)**, often called **voltage**, between two points is the energy moved per coulomb of charge:

`V = W / Q`  (unit: volt, V, where 1 V = 1 J/C)

**Capacitors and capacitance:** A **capacitor** is a device that stores electric charge. It is usually two metal plates separated by an insulator. The **capacitance** measures how much charge it stores per volt:

`C = Q / V`

where **C** = capacitance in **farads (F)**, **Q** = stored charge (C), **V** = voltage across it (V). One farad is very large, so we often use microfarads (1 µF = 10⁻⁶ F).

sections.title: Worked example: force between two charges
sections.body:
**Problem:** Two small charges, `q₁ = +2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C` and `q₂ = +3.0 × 10⁻⁶ C`, are placed **0.20 m** apart. Find the force between them. Use k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

**Step 1 — Write Coulomb's law.**
`F = k × (q₁ × q₂) / r²`

**Step 2 — Substitute the values.**
`F = (9.0 × 10⁹) × (2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁶) / (0.20)²`

**Step 3 — Work out the top.**
`2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 6.0 × 10⁻¹²`
`(9.0 × 10⁹) × (6.0 × 10⁻¹²) = 54 × 10⁻³ = 0.054`

**Step 4 — Work out the bottom.**
`(0.20)² = 0.040`

**Step 5 — Divide.**
`F = 0.054 / 0.040 = 1.35 N`

**Answer:** The force is about **1.35 N**, and because both charges are positive, it is a **repulsive** (pushing apart) force.

sections.title: A simple charged capacitor
sections.body: A capacitor connected to a battery stores charge on its two plates. The 6 V battery pushes charge onto the plates until the voltage across the capacitor equals the battery voltage. The larger the capacitance, the more charge it holds at that voltage.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Forgetting to square the distance.** Coulomb's law has `r²` in the denominator, not `r`. Always square the separation.
- **Mixing up the powers of ten.** Charges are usually micro-coulombs (10⁻⁶ C). Convert carefully before substituting.
- **Confusing attraction and repulsion.** Like charges *repel*; unlike charges *attract*. The sign of the charges tells you the direction.
- **Mixing up field (E) and potential (V).** Field is *force per charge* (N/C); potential is *energy per charge* (J/C = V).
- **Confusing the capacitor formula.** Capacitance is C = Q/V, not V/Q. A bigger capacitor stores *more* charge at the same voltage.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **"Opposites attract, likes repel"** — same as magnets and even friendships!
- For Coulomb's law remember **"k q q over r-squared"** — say it like a little rhyme.
- The constant **k ≈ 9 × 10⁹** is easy: just remember **"nine billion."**
- For capacitance use **"Q = CV"** (the "queen of capacitors"): rearrange to get C = Q/V or V = Q/C.
- Field lines: **arrows out of positive, into negative** — think of positive as a *source* (like a sprinkler) and negative as a *sink* (like a drain).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** Two charges of +4 µC and −4 µC are placed near each other. Do they attract or repel?

**Q2.** A capacitor stores 12 µC of charge when connected to a 6 V battery. What is its capacitance?

**Q3.** The electric field at a point is 200 N/C. What force acts on a charge of 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ C placed there?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** They have opposite signs, so they **attract**.
- **A2.** `C = Q/V = 12 × 10⁻⁶ / 6 = 2 × 10⁻⁶ F =` **2 µF**.
- **A3.** `F = E × q = 200 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ =` **1.0 × 10⁻³ N (0.001 N)**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- There are **two types of charge**: positive and negative. **Like charges repel, unlike attract.**
- Charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**.
- **Coulomb's law:** `F = k q₁q₂ / r²`, with k ≈ 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². It is an **inverse-square** law.
- An **electric field** strength is `E = F/q` (N/C); lines go out of positive and into negative charges.
- **Potential difference (voltage)** is energy per charge: `V = W/Q` (volts).
- A **capacitor** stores charge; **capacitance** `C = Q/V` is measured in **farads (F)**.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: A basic property of matter that causes electric forces; measured in coulombs (C). It can be positive or negative.
The rule that the force between two point charges is F = k q₁q₂ / r², proportional to the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
The region around a charge where another charge feels a force; its strength is the force per unit charge, E = F/q.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, V = W/Q, measured in volts.
A device that stores electric charge, usually two conducting plates separated by an insulator.
A measure of how much charge a capacitor stores per volt, C = Q/V, measured in farads (F).

flashcards.back: Like charges repel; unlike (opposite) charges attract.

flashcards.front: Write Coulomb's law.
flashcards.back: F = k q₁q₂ / r², where k ≈ 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

flashcards.front: What is electric field strength and its unit?
flashcards.back: Force per unit positive charge, E = F/q, measured in newtons per coulomb (N/C).

flashcards.front: What is potential difference (voltage)?
flashcards.back: The energy transferred per coulomb of charge, V = W/Q, measured in volts (V).

flashcards.front: Define capacitance and give its formula.
flashcards.back: How much charge a capacitor stores per volt: C = Q/V, measured in farads (F).

questions.prompt: Two objects both carry a positive charge. What force acts between them?
questions.explanation: Like charges repel each other, so two positively charged objects push apart.

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
questions.explanation: Electric charge is measured in coulombs (C). The volt is for voltage, the ampere for current, and the farad for capacitance.

questions.prompt: If the distance between two charges is doubled, the electric force between them becomes:
questions.explanation: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law (F ∝ 1/r²). Doubling r divides the force by 2² = 4, making it four times smaller.

questions.prompt: An electric field of 100 N/C acts on a charge of 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ C. What force does the charge feel?
A capacitor holds a charge of 20 µC when 4 V is applied across it. What is its capacitance?
questions.explanation: C = Q/V = 20 µC / 4 V = 5 µF.

chapters.title: Current Electricity
chapters.description: How electric charge flows in circuits, Ohm's law, resistance, electrical energy, power, and safety.

lessons.title: Electric Current, Ohm's Law and Power
lessons.summary: Learn what electric current is, how Ohm's law links voltage, current and resistance, and how to calculate electrical energy and power.

sections.title: Electricity that flows
sections.body:
In the last unit, charges stayed still. Now we let them **move**. When charge flows through a wire, we call it an **electric current** — the same current that lights the lamps in your home and charges a mobile phone.

Think of an electric circuit like the water pipes in a town. The **battery** is like a pump that pushes water, the **wires** are the pipes, and a **resistor** (such as a lamp) is a narrow section that the water struggles to pass through. Understanding how voltage, current, and resistance work together lets us design and use circuits safely.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Define **electric current** and state its unit.
- State and use **Ohm's law**, `V = IR`.
- Calculate the total resistance of resistors in **series** and in **parallel**.
- Explain **e.m.f.** and **internal resistance** of a cell.
- Calculate **electrical power** and **energy**.
- Describe basic **electrical safety** rules.

sections.title: Current, resistance, power, and safety
sections.body:
**Electric current (I)** is the rate of flow of electric charge:

`I = Q / t`

where **I** = current in **amperes (A)**, **Q** = charge in coulombs (C), and **t** = time in seconds. One ampere is one coulomb per second.

**Potential difference (V)** is the energy given to each coulomb of charge by the battery, measured in **volts (V)**.

**Resistance (R)** measures how much a component opposes the flow of current. Its unit is the **ohm (Ω)**.

**Ohm's law** links these three: for many conductors at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the voltage:

`V = I × R`

You can rearrange this to `I = V/R` or `R = V/I`.

**Resistors in series** (connected end to end): the current is the same through each, and resistances add up:
`R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …`

**Resistors in parallel** (connected side by side): the voltage is the same across each, and the total resistance is found from:
`1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …`
The combined resistance is always *smaller* than the smallest single resistor.

**E.m.f. and internal resistance:** A real cell is not perfect. Its **electromotive force (e.m.f., symbol ε)** is the total energy it gives per coulomb. But the cell itself has a small **internal resistance (r)**, so some energy is lost inside it. The useful voltage at the terminals is:
`V = ε − I r`

**Electrical power (P)** is the rate at which electrical energy is used:
`P = V × I`  (unit: watt, W)
Using Ohm's law, this can also be written `P = I²R` or `P = V²/R`.

**Electrical energy (E)** used over a time t is:
`E = P × t = V × I × t`  (unit: joule, J)

**Safety:** Electricity can be dangerous. Key rules include: use the correct **fuse**, **earth** metal appliances, never touch sockets with wet hands, and switch off the supply before repairs. In Ethiopia the mains supply is about **220 V**, which can give a fatal shock.

sections.title: Worked example: a lamp in a circuit
sections.body:
**Problem:** A lamp is connected to a **12 V** battery and a current of **0.5 A** flows through it. Find (a) the resistance of the lamp, and (b) the power it uses.

**Part (a) — Resistance using Ohm's law.**
`R = V / I`
`R = 12 / 0.5`
`R = 24 Ω`
So the lamp has a resistance of **24 Ω**.

**Part (b) — Power.**
`P = V × I`
`P = 12 × 0.5`
`P = 6 W`
So the lamp uses **6 watts** of power.

**Extra:** How much energy does it use in 1 minute (60 s)?
`E = P × t = 6 × 60 = 360 J`
The lamp converts **360 joules** of electrical energy in one minute.

sections.title: A simple series circuit
sections.body: This circuit shows a battery driving current through a single resistor (such as a lamp). The battery provides the voltage that pushes the current around the loop, and the resistor controls how much current flows according to Ohm's law.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Confusing the series and parallel rules.** In **series** resistances simply add. In **parallel** you must add the *reciprocals* (1/R), then flip the answer.
- **Forgetting to invert in parallel.** After working out `1/R_total`, you must take the reciprocal to get R_total itself.
- **Mixing up the units of time.** Current is charge per *second*; convert minutes to seconds before using I = Q/t.
- **Believing parallel resistance is bigger.** Adding a resistor in parallel always *decreases* the total resistance.
- **Forgetting internal resistance.** The terminal voltage of a real battery is less than its e.m.f. when current flows: V = ε − Ir.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **The "VIR triangle"**: write V on top, I and R on the bottom. Cover the one you want — V = IR, I = V/R, R = V/I.
- **"Series = Sum"** — both start with S, so in series you just add the resistances.
- For power, remember **"P = VI, the power twins"**; and the two cousins P = I²R and P = V²/R.
- **"Twinkle" for energy**: Energy = Power × time.
- Parallel resistors: think **"more paths, less resistance"** — extra roads let more cars (current) through.

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A current of 2 A flows through a 5 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?

**Q2.** Two resistors of 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?

**Q3.** An electric heater uses 220 V and draws 5 A. What is its power?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `V = IR = 2 × 5 =` **10 V**.
- **A2.** Series: `R = 3 + 6 =` **9 Ω**.
- **A3.** `P = VI = 220 × 5 =` **1100 W (1.1 kW)**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- **Electric current** `I = Q/t` is the rate of flow of charge, measured in **amperes (A)**.
- **Ohm's law:** `V = IR`. Resistance is measured in **ohms (Ω)**.
- **Series:** resistances add (`R = R₁ + R₂`). **Parallel:** `1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂`, giving a smaller total.
- A real cell has **e.m.f. ε** and **internal resistance r**, so `V = ε − Ir`.
- **Power:** `P = VI = I²R = V²/R`, in **watts (W)**. **Energy:** `E = Pt`, in **joules (J)**.
- Follow **safety rules**: correct fuse, earthing, dry hands, switch off before repairs.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: The rate of flow of electric charge, I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A).
A measure of how strongly a component opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω).
For a conductor at constant temperature, voltage equals current times resistance: V = IR.
The total energy a cell gives to each coulomb of charge, measured in volts.
The small resistance inside a cell that causes energy to be lost within the cell itself.
The rate at which electrical energy is transferred, P = VI, measured in watts (W).

flashcards.front: What is electric current and its unit?
flashcards.back: The rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A).

flashcards.front: State Ohm's law.
flashcards.back: V = IR — voltage equals current times resistance (for a conductor at constant temperature).

flashcards.front: How do you find total resistance in series?
flashcards.back: Add the resistances: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …

flashcards.front: How do you find total resistance in parallel?
flashcards.back: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … then take the reciprocal. The total is smaller than any single resistor.

flashcards.front: Give three formulas for electrical power.
flashcards.back: P = VI, P = I²R, and P = V²/R, all in watts (W).

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: Current is measured in amperes (A), where one ampere equals one coulomb of charge flowing per second.

questions.prompt: A 6 V battery drives a current of 3 A through a resistor. What is the resistance?
questions.explanation: Using R = V/I = 6/3 = 2 Ω.

questions.prompt: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: In series, resistances simply add: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω.

questions.prompt: Two 4 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: For two equal resistors in parallel, R_total = R/2 = 4/2 = 2 Ω. (1/R = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω.)

questions.prompt: A device with resistance 10 Ω carries a current of 3 A. What power does it dissipate?
questions.explanation: Using P = I²R = 3² × 10 = 9 × 10 = 90 W.

questions.prompt: A cell has an e.m.f. of 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω. When it supplies a current of 1 A, what is the terminal voltage?
questions.explanation: Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir = 1.5 − (1 × 0.5) = 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 V.

chapters.title: Electromagnetism
chapters.description: The link between electricity and magnetism: magnetic fields, magnetic forces, and electromagnetic induction.

lessons.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetic Induction
lessons.summary: Explore magnetic fields, the force on a current in a magnetic field, and how a changing magnetic field can generate electricity.

sections.title: Magnets and moving charges
sections.body:
You have probably played with a **magnet** and felt it pull on iron nails or stick to a fridge door. Magnetism and electricity may seem like separate ideas, but they are deeply connected. This connection — called **electromagnetism** — is one of the most important discoveries in physics.

A moving electric charge (a current) creates a **magnetic field**. And, amazingly, a changing magnetic field can push charges to create a current. This two-way relationship is how electric motors spin and how power stations generate the electricity that reaches Ethiopian homes.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Describe the **magnetic field** around a magnet and a current-carrying wire.
- State that a current in a magnetic field experiences a **force**.
- Use the formula `F = BIL` for the force on a wire.
- Explain **electromagnetic induction**.
- State **Faraday's law** and **Lenz's law** in simple terms.
- Describe how a **generator** produces electricity.

sections.title: Magnetic fields, forces, and induction
sections.body:
**Magnetic poles:** Every magnet has a **north pole (N)** and a **south pole (S)**. Like poles **repel**, unlike poles **attract** — just like electric charges.

**Magnetic field:** The region around a magnet where its force can be felt is the **magnetic field**. We draw it using **field lines** that run from **N to S** outside the magnet. The closer the lines, the stronger the field. The strength of the field is called the **magnetic flux density (B)**, measured in **tesla (T)**.

**Field around a current:** A wire carrying current is surrounded by a circular magnetic field. This was discovered by Oersted when a compass needle moved near a current. Wrapping the wire into a coil (a **solenoid**) makes a strong, magnet-like field — this is an **electromagnet**.

**Force on a current-carrying wire:** When a wire carrying current sits in a magnetic field, it feels a **force** (this is the *motor effect*). The size of the force is:

`F = B × I × L`

where **F** = force (N), **B** = magnetic flux density (T), **I** = current (A), and **L** = length of wire in the field (m). The force is greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field. The direction is given by **Fleming's left-hand rule**.

**Electromagnetic induction:** If you move a magnet near a coil of wire (or move the wire near a magnet), a voltage — and therefore a current — is produced in the wire. This is **electromagnetic induction**. No battery is needed; the movement does the work.

**Faraday's law:** The size of the induced voltage (e.m.f.) increases when:
- the magnet moves **faster**,
- the field is **stronger**, or
- the coil has **more turns**.
In short, a *faster change* in magnetic field through the coil gives a *bigger* induced e.m.f.

**Lenz's law:** The induced current always flows in a direction that **opposes the change** that caused it. This is really a statement of the conservation of energy.

**Generators:** A **generator** uses induction to make electricity. A coil is spun inside a magnetic field; as it turns, the magnetic field through it keeps changing, inducing an alternating voltage. Hydroelectric stations such as those on Ethiopia's rivers spin huge generators this way.

sections.title: Worked example: force on a wire
sections.body:
**Problem:** A straight wire of length **0.20 m** carries a current of **3.0 A**. It lies at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density **0.50 T**. Find the force on the wire.

**Step 1 — Write the formula.**
`F = B × I × L`

**Step 2 — Substitute the values.**
`F = 0.50 × 3.0 × 0.20`

**Step 3 — Multiply step by step.**
`0.50 × 3.0 = 1.5`
`1.5 × 0.20 = 0.30`

**Answer:** The force on the wire is **0.30 N**.

**Note:** Because the wire is at right angles (90°) to the field, this is the *maximum* possible force. If the wire were parallel to the field, the force would be zero.

sections.title: Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet
sections.body: The diagram below shows the magnetic field around a bar magnet. The field lines leave the **north pole (N)**, curve around the outside, and enter the **south pole (S)**. Where the lines are closest together (near the poles) the field is strongest.

visual.alt: A bar magnet with curved field lines running from the north pole around to the south pole; lines are densest near each pole.
visual.caption: Magnetic field lines run from N to S outside a bar magnet.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Thinking a steady magnet induces a current.** Induction needs a **changing** magnetic field. A magnet held still next to a coil produces **no** current.
- **Forgetting the right angle in F = BIL.** This formula gives the full force only when the wire is perpendicular to the field. Parallel to the field, the force is zero.
- **Confusing attract and repel for poles.** Like poles (N–N or S–S) repel; unlike poles (N–S) attract.
- **Drawing field lines the wrong way.** Outside a magnet, field lines always go from **north to south**.
- **Ignoring Lenz's law direction.** The induced current opposes the change that made it; it does not help the change.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **Fleming's left hand = force (motor):** thu**M**b = **M**otion (force), **F**irst finger = **F**ield, se**C**ond finger = **C**urrent.
- **"BIL"** sounds like a name — *Bill* the wire feels a force F = BIL.
- Field lines: **"North to South on the outside"** — they leave from N like water from a fountain.
- **Lenz = Lazy/opposing:** the induced current is "unhappy" and fights the change.
- **Faraday's recipe for a bigger voltage: "faster, stronger, more turns."**

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** Bring two north poles of magnets close together. Do they attract or repel?

**Q2.** A wire of length 0.5 m carries 4 A at right angles to a field of 0.2 T. What is the force on it?

**Q3.** Name three ways to increase the voltage induced in a coil by a moving magnet.

**Answers:**
- **A1.** Like poles **repel**.
- **A2.** `F = BIL = 0.2 × 4 × 0.5 =` **0.4 N**.
- **A3.** Move the magnet **faster**, use a **stronger** magnet, and use a coil with **more turns**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- Magnets have **north and south poles**; like poles repel, unlike attract.
- A **magnetic field** is shown by lines from **N to S**; its strength is **flux density B** in **tesla (T)**.
- A current creates a magnetic field; a coil (solenoid) makes an **electromagnet**.
- A current in a field feels a force: `F = BIL` (max when wire ⟂ field). Direction from **Fleming's left-hand rule**.
- **Electromagnetic induction:** a *changing* magnetic field induces a voltage.
- **Faraday:** faster/stronger/more turns → bigger e.m.f. **Lenz:** induced current opposes the change.
- **Generators** use induction to produce electricity.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: The region around a magnet or current where a magnetic force can be felt, shown by field lines from north to south.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
The force experienced by a current-carrying wire placed in a magnetic field, F = BIL.
The production of a voltage (and current) in a conductor by a changing magnetic field.
The induced e.m.f. is larger when the magnetic field through a coil changes faster, is stronger, or links more turns.
The induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it (conservation of energy).

flashcards.front: How do magnetic poles interact?
flashcards.back: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

flashcards.front: What is the formula for the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
flashcards.back: F = BIL, where B is flux density (T), I is current (A), and L is length (m); maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

flashcards.front: What is electromagnetic induction?
flashcards.back: The production of a voltage (and current) in a conductor by a changing magnetic field.

flashcards.front: State Lenz's law.
flashcards.back: The induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change that caused it.

flashcards.front: Name three ways to increase induced e.m.f.
flashcards.back: Move the magnet faster, use a stronger magnet, and use a coil with more turns.

questions.prompt: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another?
questions.explanation: Unlike poles attract each other, so a north and a south pole pull together.

questions.prompt: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do magnetic field lines point?
questions.explanation: By convention, magnetic field lines run from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet.

questions.prompt: A 0.40 m wire carries 5.0 A at right angles to a 0.30 T field. What is the force on it?
A magnet is held completely still inside a coil of wire. What current is induced?
questions.explanation: Induction requires a changing magnetic field. A stationary magnet produces no change, so no current is induced.

questions.prompt: Which change would NOT increase the voltage induced in a coil by a moving magnet?
options: Adding more turns to the coil
Holding the magnet still closer to the coil
questions.explanation: Holding the magnet still produces no change in field, so no voltage is induced. The other three all increase the rate of change and thus the induced e.m.f.

questions.prompt: Lenz's law states that the induced current flows in a direction that:
options: Helps the change that caused it
Opposes the change that caused it
questions.explanation: Lenz's law says the induced current always opposes the change producing it, which is a consequence of the conservation of energy.

chapters.title: Introduction to Electronics
chapters.description: The basics of electronics: vacuum tubes, conductors, insulators, semiconductors, doping, and transistors.

lessons.title: Semiconductors and Transistors
lessons.summary: Learn how materials are classed by how well they conduct, how doping creates semiconductors, and how diodes and transistors work.

sections.title: The heart of modern devices
sections.body:
Every mobile phone, radio, television, and computer relies on **electronics**. At the centre of these devices are tiny components made from special materials called **semiconductors**.

Long ago, electronics used large, hot, fragile **vacuum tubes**. Today these have been replaced by small, reliable **transistors** made from semiconductors like silicon. Understanding how these materials and components work helps explain how the technology around us actually functions.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Describe what a **vacuum tube** does in simple terms.
- Classify materials as **conductors**, **insulators**, or **semiconductors**.
- Explain how **doping** changes a semiconductor into **n-type** or **p-type**.
- Describe how a **diode** allows current in only one direction.
- Describe the basic structure and use of a **transistor** (npn and pnp).

sections.title: Conductors, semiconductors, doping, and transistors
sections.body:
**Vacuum tubes:** A **vacuum tube** is a sealed glass tube with the air removed. Inside, a heated part releases electrons that flow to a positive plate. Early tubes (called diodes and triodes) were used to control and amplify electrical signals, but they were bulky and used a lot of power.

**Conductors, insulators, semiconductors:** Materials are grouped by how easily electric current passes through them:
- **Conductors** (e.g. copper, aluminium) let current flow easily because they have many free electrons.
- **Insulators** (e.g. rubber, glass, plastic) hardly let any current flow.
- **Semiconductors** (e.g. **silicon**, **germanium**) are in between. They conduct only a little when pure, but their conduction can be controlled — which makes them extremely useful.

**Doping:** Pure silicon is a poor conductor. By adding tiny amounts of other elements — a process called **doping** — we change how it conducts:
- **n-type:** adding an element with extra electrons (e.g. phosphorus) gives free **negative** charge carriers (electrons).
- **p-type:** adding an element with fewer electrons (e.g. boron) creates **"holes"** that behave like positive charge carriers.

**The p-n junction (diode):** When a piece of p-type material is joined to n-type material, it forms a **p-n junction**, which is a **diode**. A diode lets current flow **easily in one direction** (called *forward bias*) but blocks it in the other direction (*reverse bias*). This makes diodes useful for converting alternating current to direct current.

**Transistors:** A **transistor** is made of three doped layers. There are two types:
- **npn** (n-type, p-type, n-type)
- **pnp** (p-type, n-type, p-type)
The three parts are called the **emitter**, **base**, and **collector**. A small current into the base controls a much larger current between the collector and emitter. This means a transistor can act as:
- an **amplifier** (making a small signal larger), or
- a **switch** (turning a current on or off).

Transistors are the building blocks of all modern computer chips, where billions of them work together.

sections.title: Worked example: identifying materials and behaviour
sections.body:
**Problem:** A student tests three materials in a simple circuit with a battery and a bulb. With material A the bulb is bright; with material B it does not light at all; with material C the bulb glows faintly and gets brighter when the material is warmed. Classify each material and explain.

**Step 1 — Material A (bulb bright).** Current flows easily, so it has many free electrons. **Material A is a conductor** (such as copper).

**Step 2 — Material B (no light).** Almost no current flows, so it has very few free charge carriers. **Material B is an insulator** (such as plastic or glass).

**Step 3 — Material C (faint glow, brighter when warm).** It conducts only a little, and warming it increases conduction. This is the signature behaviour of a **semiconductor** (such as silicon): heat frees more charge carriers, so conduction rises with temperature.

**Conclusion:** A = conductor, B = insulator, C = semiconductor. The temperature test is the key clue that C is a semiconductor, since unlike metals, semiconductors conduct *better* when heated.

sections.title: A diode in a circuit
sections.body: This circuit shows a diode connected to a battery. In **forward bias** (as drawn) the diode allows current to flow and the lamp lights. If the battery were reversed, the diode would block the current and the lamp would stay off.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Thinking semiconductors behave like metals.** In metals, conduction *drops* when heated; in semiconductors, conduction *rises* when heated. They are different.
- **Believing "holes" are real particles.** A **hole** is simply a missing electron that behaves like a positive charge. It is a useful idea, not an actual particle.
- **Mixing up n-type and p-type.** **n-type has extra electrons (negative carriers); p-type has holes (positive carriers).** The letter hints at the charge.
- **Thinking a diode conducts both ways.** A diode conducts in **one direction only** (forward bias).
- **Confusing the transistor parts.** The small **base** current controls the large current between **collector** and **emitter**.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- **n-type = Negative carriers (electrons); p-type = Positive carriers (holes).** The letter matches the charge.
- **Diode = "one-way door"** for current — it only opens in the forward direction.
- **Doping = adding a tiny "dose"** of impurity to change conduction.
- Transistor parts: **"E-B-C" → Emitter, Base, Collector** (think "every basic chip").
- A transistor is like a **tap**: a small turn of the handle (base current) controls a big flow of water (collector current).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** Name two common semiconductor materials.

**Q2.** What type of charge carrier is added when silicon is doped to make it n-type?

**Q3.** In which direction does a diode allow current to flow easily?

**Answers:**
- **A1.** **Silicon** and **germanium**.
- **A2.** Extra **electrons** (negative charge carriers).
- **A3.** In the **forward** direction (forward bias) only.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- Early electronics used **vacuum tubes**; modern electronics use **semiconductors**.
- Materials are **conductors** (easy flow), **insulators** (almost no flow), or **semiconductors** (in between, controllable).
- **Silicon** and **germanium** are common semiconductors.
- **Doping** makes **n-type** (extra electrons) or **p-type** (holes) material.
- A **diode** (p-n junction) lets current flow **one way only**.
- A **transistor** (npn or pnp) uses a small **base** current to control a large current — it works as an **amplifier** or a **switch**.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: A material that lets electric current flow easily because it has many free electrons (e.g. copper).
A material that hardly lets any current flow because it has very few free charge carriers (e.g. rubber).
A material such as silicon whose conduction is between that of a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled.
Adding tiny amounts of impurity to a semiconductor to change how it conducts, making n-type or p-type material.
A p-n junction device that allows current to flow in one direction only.
A three-layer semiconductor device (npn or pnp) in which a small base current controls a larger current; used as an amplifier or switch.

flashcards.front: Name the three classes of materials by how they conduct electricity.
flashcards.back: Conductors (easy flow), insulators (almost no flow), and semiconductors (in between, controllable).

flashcards.front: What is doping?
flashcards.back: Adding a tiny amount of impurity to a semiconductor to change its conduction, creating n-type or p-type material.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between n-type and p-type semiconductors?
flashcards.back: n-type has extra free electrons (negative carriers); p-type has holes (positive carriers).

flashcards.front: What does a diode do?
flashcards.back: It allows current to flow in one direction only (forward bias) and blocks it in the other.

flashcards.front: How does a transistor work?
flashcards.back: A small current into the base controls a much larger current between collector and emitter, acting as an amplifier or a switch.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best example of an electrical conductor?
questions.explanation: Copper is a metal with many free electrons, so it conducts electricity easily. The others are insulators.

questions.prompt: Which material is a common semiconductor used in electronics?
questions.explanation: Silicon (along with germanium) is a widely used semiconductor. Copper and aluminium are conductors, and plastic is an insulator.

questions.prompt: Doping silicon to create n-type material adds which kind of charge carrier?
questions.explanation: n-type material is made by adding impurities that provide extra free electrons, which are negative charge carriers.

questions.prompt: What is the main property of a diode?
options: It allows current in one direction only
questions.explanation: A diode is a p-n junction that allows current to flow easily in the forward direction but blocks it in the reverse direction.

questions.prompt: How does the electrical conduction of a pure semiconductor change as its temperature increases?
questions.explanation: Unlike metals, semiconductors conduct better when heated because heat frees more charge carriers.

questions.prompt: In a transistor, a small current into which terminal controls a much larger current?
questions.explanation: A small base current controls the much larger current flowing between the collector and emitter, allowing the transistor to amplify or switch.

chapters.title: Electromagnetic Waves and Geometrical Optics
chapters.description: The nature of electromagnetic waves and how light behaves when it is reflected and refracted.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Waves, Reflection and Refraction
lessons.summary: Understand the electromagnetic spectrum, the law of reflection, and how light bends when it changes speed (refraction).

sections.title: Light and invisible waves
sections.body:
Light lets you see this page, but light is just one small part of a much larger family of waves called **electromagnetic (EM) waves**. Radio signals, microwaves, X-rays, and the warmth you feel from the Sun are all EM waves too.

**Optics** is the study of light. In this lesson we look at two everyday behaviours of light: **reflection** (bouncing off surfaces, like a mirror) and **refraction** (bending when it passes from one material into another, like a straw that looks broken in a glass of water).

sections.title: What you will be able to do
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Describe **electromagnetic waves** and list parts of the **EM spectrum**.
- State that all EM waves travel at the **speed of light** in a vacuum.
- Use the wave equation `v = fλ`.
- State and use the **law of reflection**.
- Explain **refraction** and use **Snell's law** with the **refractive index**.

sections.title: EM waves, reflection, and refraction
sections.body:
**Electromagnetic waves** are made of vibrating electric and magnetic fields that travel together. They are **transverse waves** and, unlike sound, they can travel through empty space (a vacuum).

**Speed of light:** All EM waves travel through a vacuum at the same enormous speed:
`c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s`

**The EM spectrum:** EM waves are grouped by their wavelength and frequency. From longest wavelength (lowest frequency) to shortest:
**radio waves → microwaves → infrared → visible light → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays.**
Visible light is the only part our eyes can see, running from red (longest) to violet (shortest).

**The wave equation** links speed, frequency, and wavelength for any wave:
`v = f × λ`
where **v** = speed (m/s), **f** = frequency (Hz), and **λ** (lambda) = wavelength (m).

**Reflection:** When light hits a smooth surface it bounces off. We measure angles from the **normal** — an imaginary line at right angles to the surface. The **law of reflection** states:
`angle of incidence = angle of reflection`
The incoming ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane.

**Refraction:** When light passes from one transparent material into another (say from air into water), it changes **speed** and usually **bends**. Light bends *toward* the normal when it slows down (entering a denser material) and *away* from the normal when it speeds up.

**Refractive index (n):** This number tells us how much a material slows light down:
`n = (speed of light in vacuum) / (speed of light in the material) = c / v`
A larger n means light travels more slowly and bends more. For example, water has n ≈ 1.33 and glass n ≈ 1.5.

**Snell's law** gives the exact bending:
`n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂`
where θ₁ is the angle in the first material and θ₂ is the angle in the second.

sections.title: Worked example: refraction into glass
sections.body:
**Problem:** Light travels from air (n₁ = 1.0) into glass (n₂ = 1.5). It strikes the surface at an **angle of incidence of 30°**. Find the **angle of refraction** inside the glass.

**Step 1 — Write Snell's law.**
`n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂`

**Step 2 — Substitute the known values.**
`1.0 × sin 30° = 1.5 × sin θ₂`

**Step 3 — Work out the left side.**
`sin 30° = 0.5`, so the left side = `1.0 × 0.5 = 0.5`.

**Step 4 — Solve for sin θ₂.**
`0.5 = 1.5 × sin θ₂`
`sin θ₂ = 0.5 / 1.5 = 0.333`

**Step 5 — Find the angle.**
`θ₂ = sin⁻¹(0.333) ≈ 19.5°`

**Answer:** The angle of refraction is about **19.5°**. Notice the angle got *smaller* — the light bent **toward the normal** because it slowed down entering the denser glass.

sections.title: Reflection of light at a mirror
sections.body: The diagram shows a ray of light hitting a flat mirror. The **normal** is drawn at right angles to the surface. The **angle of incidence** (between the incoming ray and the normal) always equals the **angle of reflection** (between the reflected ray and the normal).

visual.alt: A light ray hitting a horizontal mirror, with a dashed normal line; the angle of incidence on one side of the normal equals the angle of reflection on the other side.
visual.caption: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

sections.title: Mistakes students often make
sections.body:
- **Measuring angles from the surface.** All angles in optics are measured from the **normal** (the perpendicular line), not from the surface itself.
- **Thinking light always bends the same way.** Light bends **toward** the normal when entering a *denser* material and **away** when entering a *less dense* one.
- **Mixing up the refractive index formula.** It is `n = c/v` (vacuum speed over material speed), so n is always **greater than 1** for normal materials.
- **Forgetting units in v = fλ.** Frequency is in hertz (Hz) and wavelength in metres (m).
- **Confusing reflection and refraction.** Reflection is *bouncing off*; refraction is *bending while passing through*.

sections.title: Tricks to remember it
sections.body:
- EM spectrum order: **"Real Monsters Invade Very Unusual X-ray Games"** → Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-ray, Gamma.
- Reflection rule is simply **"i = r"** (incidence equals reflection).
- **"Slow = toward, fast = away"** for refraction: light slowing bends *toward* the normal.
- Refractive index: **"n = c over v"**, and remember **"n is never less than 1"** for ordinary materials.
- Speed of light: memorise **"3 times ten to the eight"** (3 × 10⁸ m/s).

sections.title: Practice questions
sections.body:
Try these, then check the answers below.

**Q1.** A wave has frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is its wavelength?

**Q2.** A light ray hits a mirror at an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of reflection?

**Q3.** Light travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a certain glass. What is the refractive index of the glass? (Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.)

**Answers:**
- **A1.** `λ = v/f = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m` (600 nm).
- **A2.** By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection = **40°**.
- **A3.** `n = c/v = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 2.0 × 10⁸ =` **1.5**.

sections.title: Key points
sections.body:
- **EM waves** are transverse waves of electric and magnetic fields that travel through a vacuum at `c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s`.
- The **EM spectrum** (long to short): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
- Wave equation: `v = fλ`.
- **Law of reflection:** angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
- **Refraction** is the bending of light when its speed changes; it bends **toward** the normal in a denser medium.
- **Refractive index** `n = c/v`; **Snell's law:** `n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂`.

sections.title: Key words
sections.body: Important terms from this lesson.

glossary.definition: A transverse wave of vibrating electric and magnetic fields that can travel through a vacuum at the speed of light.
The full range of EM waves arranged by wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
An imaginary line drawn at right angles to a surface, used to measure angles in reflection and refraction.
The rule that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
The bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another and changes speed.
A number showing how much a material slows light, n = c/v; the larger it is, the more the light bends.

flashcards.front: What is the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum?
flashcards.back: About 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s (the speed of light, c).

flashcards.front: List the EM spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength.
flashcards.back: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma rays.

flashcards.front: State the law of reflection.
flashcards.back: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

flashcards.front: What is the refractive index formula?
flashcards.back: n = c/v, the speed of light in a vacuum divided by its speed in the material.

flashcards.front: Write Snell's law of refraction.
flashcards.back: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate speed of light (and all EM waves) in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at about 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of light.

questions.prompt: Which of these EM waves has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Radio waves have the longest wavelength (and lowest frequency) of the listed waves; gamma rays have the shortest.

questions.prompt: A ray of light strikes a flat mirror with an angle of incidence of 25°. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is 25°.

questions.prompt: A wave travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s with a wavelength of 3.0 m. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Rearranging v = fλ gives f = v/λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 3.0 = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz.

questions.prompt: When light passes from air into glass (a denser medium), how does it bend?
questions.explanation: Light slows down entering the denser glass, so it bends toward the normal.

questions.prompt: Light travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s inside a transparent material. Using c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, what is the refractive index?
